claims.text: Replacing EAM and thermodynamic integration with an MTP-plus-FEP workflow will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP-plus-FEP workflow will agree with TOR-TILD to within 0.5 meV/atom in free energy.
Maintaining the stated accuracy requires the MTP to capture the SRO stabilization contribution.
TaVCrW is initially a disordered BCC solid solution at 0 K.
The baseline DFT calculation neglects electronic-excitation effects and magnetic fluctuations.
FEP is used to calculate the Gibbs free-energy difference between the solid and liquid phases.
The proposed workflow is to be evaluated over 2000-2400 K.
A supercell containing more than 100 atoms is likely sufficient to capture SRO correlations and limit finite-size effects.
The MTP must be trained on a diverse phase-space distribution containing both solid and liquid configurations.
Accurate reproduction of ab initio phase-space distributions, local atomic environments, and SRO is the structural mediator that makes FEP valid.
SRO contributes approximately 2-3 meV/atom of stabilization energy in the solid.
The MTP acts as a computationally efficient surrogate for the DFT energy landscape.
The computational efficiency of the MTP permits the extensive phase-space sampling required by FEP.
FEP obtains free-energy differences by exponential averaging of energy differences between the MTP and a reference state.
Using FEP bypasses the slow convergence associated with thermodynamic integration.
FEP accuracy depends on the MTP reproducing SRO and the relevant electronic environments, including possible V/Cr underbinding or overbinding anomalies.
The method will correctly predict the SRO contribution to solid-phase stability.
TOR-TILD is expensive because it requires extensive sampling and explicit DFT calculations along the integration path.
The hypothesis applies only when the 2000-2400 K range does not introduce magnetic or electronic effects absent from the MTP training.
Failure to model electronic or magnetic free-energy contributions may cause the FEP discrepancy to exceed 0.5 meV/atom.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says that the melting temperature will differ by less than 0.5 meV/atom. Melting-temperature differences require temperature units, whereas 0.5 meV/atom is a free-energy tolerance. The parenthetical clarification does not fully resolve this category mismatch.
